Italian Renaissance: One-Point Perspective

📖 TODAY'S FOCUS
How do artists make a flat sheet of paper look deep and real?
During the Renaissance, Italian artists found a way to turn a flat surface into a window with real depth. They called the system linear perspective. The simplest kind, one-point perspective, uses a single point in the distance to organize a whole scene. Today you learn the three parts that make it work, then you put them to use building your own city.
✅ BY THE END OF THIS MODULE, YOU WILL BE ABLE TO
☐ Name and use the three parts of one-point perspective: the horizon line, the vanishing point, and orthogonal lines.
☐ Explain how Renaissance artists used linear perspective to make flat surfaces look like real, deep space.
☐ Draw an original city scene that uses one vanishing point, then sign it as your finished, original work.
⚡ QUICK CHECK-IN
When have you seen lines seem to shrink toward one point in real life? (No wrong answer. Just check in with yourself.)
📚 PART 1 · THE THREE PARTS

Three words to build with

Before this system, most artwork looked flat, and objects did not seem the right size or distance apart. Renaissance artists wanted paintings that felt like real life, with space, distance, and depth. They built that feeling out of three simple parts.

Horizon line
A horizontal line at the viewer's eye level. It is where the ground and sky seem to meet.
Vanishing point
A single point on the horizon line where parallel lines appear to come together.
Orthogonal lines
The diagonal edges that lead back to the vanishing point. They are what show depth.
💡 THE KEY IDEA
In one-point perspective, the vanishing point always sits on the horizon line, and every orthogonal line leads to it. Things closer to you look larger; things farther away look smaller.
📚 PART 2 · WHERE IT CAME FROM

A Renaissance discovery

The Renaissance was a period in European history, roughly 1400 to 1600 A.D., often called a rebirth of art, science, and learning. Artists began studying nature, math, and the human body to make their work look more real. In the early 1400s, the Italian architect Filippo Brunelleschi used geometry to experiment with realistic space. Soon after, the painter Masaccio used one-point perspective in his fresco The Holy Trinity (1427 A.D.), where the whole scene appears to recede into deep, believable space.

Masaccio, The Holy Trinity, about 1425–1427 A.D. Santa Maria Novella, Florence. Public domain.
🔍 FIND THE PERSPECTIVE
Masaccio painted a stone archway and a barrel-vaulted ceiling that look like they cut straight back into the wall. Trace the lines of the ceiling panels: they all angle toward one spot, deep inside the painted space, right behind the cross. That spot is the vanishing point. This fresco is one of the very first artworks in Western history to use true one-point perspective, painted decades before Leonardo's Last Supper.

Later artists carried the method further. The most famous example you will study next is Leonardo da Vinci's The Last Supper, where all the lines lead your eye to one place.

👁 PART 3 · LOOK CLOSELY

Leonardo da Vinci, The Last Supper

Leonardo da Vinci painted The Last Supper on a wall in Italy, about 1495 to 1497 A.D. Thirteen figures sit along a long table in a tall room. The ceiling is divided into a grid of panels, and the side walls hold rows of tapestries that get smaller and closer together as they move back. Behind the central figure, a bright doorway and windows open onto distant hills.

🔍 FIND THE PERSPECTIVE
Trace the edges of the ceiling and the tops of the wall hangings. They are orthogonal lines, and they all angle toward one spot: the head of the figure at the center. That spot is the vanishing point, sitting on the room's horizon line. Leonardo used perspective to pull your eye straight to the most important part of the scene.
Leonardo da Vinci, The Last Supper, about 1495–1497 A.D. Public domain.
